claims.statement: Daytime sky is blue because nitrogen/oxygen molecules (much smaller than visible wavelengths) Rayleigh-scatter short-wavelength blue light much more strongly than long-wavelength red light.

claims.freshness: Textbook-level law; University of Arizona PDF and Rochester lecture are undated course notes but state the standard formula. Accessed 2026-09-26.
claims.notes: Quoted ratios differ by wavelength pair: NOAA JetStream says blue ~4x red; NASA GSFC lecture says ~9x blue-violet vs red; Rochester PHY218 computes (630/430)^4 ~ 4.6-6.1. Script should say 'several times more' not a single number.

claims.statement: Rayleigh scattering intensity scales approximately as 1/lambda^4, so blue (~400-450 nm) is scattered several times more efficiently than red (~650-700 nm).

claims.freshness: NOAA NESDIS page published 2025-08-31 per fetch; Arizona mirror of UC Riverside Baez explainer is long-standing course content. Accessed 2026-09-26.
claims.notes: Violet IS scattered even more strongly; it does not dominate perception. Ozone/Chappuis absorption nuance (ACP 2023) exists but is beyond 60s scope.

claims.statement: The sky looks blue rather than violet because sunlight contains less violet, upper-atmosphere absorption removes some violet, human eyes are less sensitive to violet than blue, and red+green cone responses blend scattered violet/indigo toward pale blue.

claims.freshness: NASA Space Place and NOAA GML pages are stable explainers; UIUC WW2010 is archived course content. All fetched 2026-09-26.

claims.statement: Sunsets/sunrises look red/orange because the low sun's light takes a much longer path through the atmosphere, so most blue/violet has been scattered away and mainly longer red-yellow wavelengths reach the eye directly.

claims.freshness: HyperPhysics and NOAA NESDIS fetched 2026-09-26; UIUC WW2010 Mie page found via search. Mechanism is textbook-stable.

claims.statement: Gas molecules cause wavelength-selective Rayleigh scattering (blue sky), while larger dust, pollution, salt, smoke and cloud droplets cause weakly wavelength-dependent Mie scattering that whitens the sky/haze and can intensify red sunsets.

claims.statement: The scattering explanation is named for Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt, 1842-1919), who published the theory in 1871 with elaborations through the 1880s-1890s.
